title: Environmental Heterogeneity and Competition Shape Intraspecific Variability of Ecological Niches in Highly Mobile Marine Species
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Among-population variability in species ecology and traits is ubiquitous across species, with consequences for species distribution in space and time, population dynamics, species resilience, coexistence or speciation. Although variability in specific ecological traits is often studied, studies at larger ecological niche scale are much less frequent. This gap results in a poor understanding of population segregation in niches and of how it changes through time or in relation to resource heterogeneity, thereby hindering our ability to predict the effects of environmental changes.

Location

Atlantic Ocean.

Time Period

Full year: 1999–2022.

Major Taxa Studied

Seabirds.

Methods

We measured the intraspecific variability in niche structure, then evaluated how niche specialisation and intraspecific segregation varied with environmental oceanographic heterogeneity, and especially so with the spatio-temporal variability of primary productivity, bathymetry, temperature and other conditions, and with the seasonality of those. We then examined how intraspecific competition altered such patterns. Segregation in space, and its intraspecific variability, was further measured and compared to that in the niche. To do so, we compiled year-round geolocation data for 12 seabird species from 73 colonies distributed across the North Atlantic Ocean, from the tropics to the Arctic, from which we quantified the ecological niches at the species and local population (colony) scales, contrasting periods of high (breeding) and low (non-breeding) intraspecific competition.

Results

We found that: (1) spatial segregation did not typically indicate environmental niche segregation, (2) niche specialisation increased in more productive and temporally stable environments, (3) niche segregation increased with higher seasonal variability in productivity, (4) competition exacerbated these patterns.

Main Conclusions

Intraspecific competition and resource heterogeneity closely interplay to shape ecological niches and spatial distributions, with temporal stability of ocean productivity and temperature playing a crucial role.
